title: Performance Optimization of Novel Laser Hybrid Ultrasonic Vibration Assisted Micro Milling for Inconel 718
abstract: Abstract Miniaturization drives advanced manufacturing essential for next-generation systems using superalloys in aerospace, biomedical and microelectronics. Hybrid machining combines distinct processes to harness their individual strengths and overcome limitations. This experimental research explored the machinability of Inconel 718 through novel laser hybrid ultrasonic vibration-assisted micro-milling (L-UVAMM), utilizing fiber laser for preparing slots followed by micro-milling on the corresponding laser-generated pilot slots with uncoated and three different coated tools. Cutting speed, feed, depth of cut, tool coatings and amplitude considered as input variables across four discrete levels to design experiments using Taguchi L-16 orthogonal array to investigate their effect on key responses including surface roughness, tool wear, and burr formation. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Grey Relational Analysis (GRA) identified the most significant parameters and determined the best input combinations. Uncoated tools displayed the least tool wear, TiSiN minimized burr height while TiAlN improved surface roughness and reduced burr width. ANOVA for the regression model revealed the tool type as the most crucial factor influencing responses with a contribution ratio of 45.76%. Response surface method optimized the regression model for optimum conditions, resulted in 43.96%, 27.18%, and 19.65% average reduction of surface roughness, tool wear, and burr formation, respectively.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Miniaturization is the driving force behind modern technological innovations, fueled by the mandate for more compact, efficient, and affordable solutions. It pointedly impacts on performance enhancement in various industries including aerospace, automotive and biomedical as well as electronics by providing compact designs for more functionality and integrating new features 1 . Mechanical micromachining can produce complex microstructures on a variety of materials, especially nickel-based alloys, with the advantages of high machining accuracy and surface integrity while diminishing tool wear. With small tool diameters, the issues associated with cutting edge geometry and tool rigidity influence workpiece accuracy and surface finish 2 , 3 . Challenging environmental conditions shaped by high temperature, mechanical stress and corrosive elements sturdily need durable superalloy 4 . In high performance systems, nickel-based alloys are especially imperative for aircraft turbines, rocket and submarine engines operating reliably at temperatures ranging from 450 to 700 °C 5 . Superalloy Inconel 718 is recognized for its unprecedented combination of high strength at elevated temperatures and excellent corrosion resistance, which guarantees structural integrity in extreme service settings 6 . Due to its excellent resistance to heat and corrosion, it is preferred choice in sectors such as power generation, gas turbines and nuclear energy systems 7 , 8 . Inconel 718 is frequently alloyed with aluminum to produce lightweight and heat-resistant structural components 9 , 10 . Numerous studies have focused on the viability of employing various energy field machining techniques to augment the machinability of these alloys 11 . Vibration-assisted machining converts continuous contact into instantaneous, intermittent and reciprocating by applying low-frequency or ultrasonic vibrations to the tool or workpiece 12 , 13 . Ultrasonic machining, characterized by vibrations above 16 kHz 14 , enhances the machinability of high-strength alloys by generating vibrations in one or multiple cutting directions. For instance, axial vibration is promising for ultrasonic assisted grinding of Inconel 718 15 . Vibration in machining facilitates chip removal, preventing re-engagement and reducing cutting forces, tool wear and burr formation 16 . The material’s physical characteristics alter, softens the material, enabling smoother cutting and better surface finish 17 , 18 . Ultrasonic Vibration-Assisted Micro-Milling (UVAMM) enhances chip breaking, inhibits burr formation, reduces friction, mitigates size and plowing effects and extends tool life while ensuring precision 19 , 20 . While effectively used in turning, drilling and grinding, K. M. Li and S. L. Wang believe that its potential in micro-milling remains unexplored and the influence of tool wear on surface roughness and burr formation remains uncertain 2 .

Ultrasonic machining offers significant advantages for machining Inconel 718 21 . Integrating ultrasonic vibrations with traditional milling offers various advantages unique to Inconel 718 by breaking chips into smaller pieces, enabling faster evacuation from the cutting zone. Vibrations minimize tool-workpiece contact, improving surface finish and reducing imperfections without extensive post-processing 22 , 23 . It allows precise machining of turbine blades with superior surface quality and dimensional accuracy in aerospace 10 , 24 . Experimental investigations by M. Xu et al. 25  show that machinability of Inconel 718 can be improved because both cutting force and temperature significantly decreased in ultrasonic machining. H. Zhang et al. concluded that unlike one-dimensional tools that vibrate in a single either tangential or axial direction, two-dimensional ultrasonic tools produce elliptical or circular motion trajectory for enhanced cutting performance 26 . Rotary ultrasonic elliptical milling which applies transverse ultrasonic vibrations, has demonstrated superior machinability for cast Ni-based superalloys 27 , 28 . Laser ultrasonic elliptical machining was conducted by M. Khajehzadeh et al., revealing the effect of vibration amplitude and feed rate on cutting forces and surface roughness 29 . Lianxing et al. proposed a novel approach using an anticlockwise vibration direction to limit the surface roughness 30 . N. Ngah et al. believe that innovative approaches like hybrid machining methods which combine ultrasonic milling with other technologies, could provide even more precision and efficiency gains 10 .

Hybrid manufacturing techniques, like additive-subtractive hybrid manufacturing based on Laser-Directed Energy Deposition, integrate additive and subtractive processes for fabricating complex Inconel 718 structural components, with reduced surface plastic deformation 31 . H. Zhou et al. employed ultrasonic vibration for the first time to assist Laser-Directed Energy Deposition milling hybrid process in manufacturing thin-walled parts of GH4169 and found that it exhibited varying surface roughness 32 . Laser beam machining alone cannot produce finished products which can be used for variety of purposes due to limitations like uncontrolled dimensions and tapered surfaces 33 . Emerging novel hybrid approaches are effective for creating micro-scale parts in difficult-to-cut materials. These methods incorporate non-conventional energy-assisted processes such as vibration, laser and electricity by considering both structural and machining characteristics of the material to improve machinability while minimizing mechanical stress during fabrication 34 . Y. Du et al. proposed a pulsed laser-assisted ultrasonic elliptical vibration cutting technique, where both processes act synergistically to improve machinability 35 . Hybrid micro-machining combines two or more processes either sequentially or in assisted configuration to enhance overall performance while minimizing drawbacks 36 , 37 . In the sequential approach, each process is performed one after another on separate systems offering greater flexibility and simpler integration in selecting and customizing operations 38 . Conversely, assisted way involves simultaneous execution, where one process supports the other, requiring precise synchronization and specialized equipment with higher initial costs. Gupta et al. reported that hybrid techniques are applied in fabricating micro-features such as micro-holes, channels and complex 3D structures in challenging materials like metals, non-metals and superalloys 39 , 40 .

Laser Assisted Machining or ablation enhances machinability by using a laser beam to locally soften or modify material with negligible damage, forming a metamorphic layer while mechanical machining removes the heat affected zone 41 , 42 . Studies on laser assisted micro-milling of Inconel 718 by H. Zhang et al. reveal moderate reduction in cutting forces 43 . Similarly, it has been applied to Niobium alloy (C-103) and concluded that laser has a substantial impact on response variables 44 . J. Dominguez-Caballero et al. found that laser ultrasonic machining process improves machinability of Ti-6Al-4 V during turning over diverse speeds and depths of cut 23 . C. Zhang et al. also did turning by integrating ultrasonic vibration with laser energy to boost tungsten carbide cutting, lifespan of CBN tools and precision machining 45 . Cemented carbide was machined using laser ultrasonic assisted milling by C. Zhang et al., improving micro-morphology while minimizing cutting forces, tool wear and surface roughness 46 .

Despite extensive independent investigations on laser-assisted machining and ultrasonic vibration-assisted micromachining, a significant research gap remains concerning their combined influence on the micro-machinability of Inconel 718. Existing laser-assisted milling investigations predominantly employ simultaneous laser heating during cutting to achieve thermal softening and cutting force reduction, while ultrasonic vibration-assisted milling is known to induce high-frequency intermittent tool–workpiece contact, improving chip formation, mitigating adhesion-driven wear, and suppressing burr formation effects that are particularly critical at the micro-scale where minimum uncut chip thickness and ploughing dominate cutting mechanics. In contrast to these single-assistance approaches, the present study introduces and experimentally evaluates a novel sequential hybrid strategy for micromachining Inconel 718, in which controlled laser ablation is first applied to condition the near-surface material state, followed by ultrasonic vibration-assisted micro-milling using both uncoated and coated micro-tools. This intentional sequence establishes modified engagement conditions that enhance intermittent cutting stability and chip-formation behavior during subsequent micro-milling. Unlike conventional simultaneous laser-assisted machining approaches primarily aimed at transient thermal softening during cutting, the proposed L-UVAMM framework employs a sequential hybrid strategy in which laser pre-conditioning establishes pilot-slot geometry in a separate stage prior to ultrasonic vibration-assisted micro-milling. Consequently, the subsequent ultrasonic stage operates on a laser-conditioned surface rather than untreated bulk material, thereby creating a distinct sequential hybrid material-removal pathway for micro-machining of Inconel 718.

This hybrid strategy synergistically combines the geometric flexibility of laser ablation with accuracy, and low thermal damage of mechanical micro-milling. Notably, the combined effects of this sequential hybrid process together with different tool coatings on surface roughness, tool wear, and burr formation have not previously examined within a single experimental framework. Bridging this gap is of considerable industrial importance for improving performance, precision, and productivity in micromachining of Inconel 718. The present work systematically addresses this gap by analyzing the effects of cutting speed, feed per tooth, depth of cut, and vibration amplitude under the proposed L-UVAMM framework. A structured Taguchi L16 orthogonal design (five factors, four levels) is employed, followed by multi-response parametric optimization and Response Surface Methodology, to establish optimal machining conditions and provide practical parameter-ranking guidance for high-quality and reliable micromachining of Inconel 718. The principal contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A novel sequential hybrid micromachining framework L-UVAMM is developed and experimentally validated for Inconel 718, integrating controlled laser ablation as a pre-conditioning stage with subsequent ultrasonic vibration-assisted micro-milling. This two-step assistance concept creates a unique, previously unreported pathway for improving machinability. A systematic experimental approach based on Taguchi L16 orthogonal array that enables comprehensive, efficient, and statistically balanced exploration of the multi-dimensional parameter space is employed to evaluate the combined effects of five key process parameters: cutting speed, feed per tooth, depth of cut, tool coating material and vibration amplitude at four distinct levels. Comprehensive multi-response evaluation is performed by simultaneously evaluating surface roughness, tool wear (flank and face wear), and burr formation (burr width and height) within a unified experimental framework with ANOVA identifying tool type as the dominant controlling factor. A comparative performance assessment of both uncoated and coated carbide micro-tools (TiAlN, TiSiN, and nACo) is conducted under identical hybrid machining conditions, offering practical reference for tool selection in high-precision micromachining of Inconel 718. An integrated multi-objective optimization framework combining Grey Relational Analysis and Response Surface Methodology is employed to determine optimal machining conditions, quantify parametric interactions, and develop predictive response surfaces for improved process planning and industrial implementation.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: An experimental investigation was conducted on hybrid technique that integrates two distinct processes for machining a workpiece. This method employed a two-step approach. The first step involved creating pilot slots using a fiber laser, followed by ultrasonic vibration-assisted mechanical micro-milling on these laser-generated pilot slots in the second step to achieve the final geometry. During UVAMM in second step, the tool is subjected to high frequency and small vibration amplitudes. The basic concept involved integration of ultrasonic vibrations into the standard milling operation. By delivering high-frequency vibrations of 20 kHz, the machine creates oscillations at micro-scale in cutting tool, which leads to chips breakup and lessen the cutting forces 16 , 47 . The scheme for experimentation and response analysis framework is outlined in Fig.  1 .
Fig. 1 Scheme of experimentation, measurement, and subsequent analysis.

Ultrasonic vibration-assisted micro-milling improves machining performance primarily through intermittent tool–workpiece contact, which reduces friction, stabilizes chip formation, and suppresses burr formation in Inconel 718 19 , 48 . However, under micro-scale cutting conditions, further performance improvement through parameter optimization alone becomes increasingly constrained by ploughing-dominated deformation, unstable chip evacuation, adhesion-driven wear, and severe full-engagement conditions during initial tool entry. In the proposed sequential framework, laser-generated pilot slots act as a pre-conditioning stage by selectively removing material along the intended cutting path through controlled laser ablation 43 . Unlike conventional simultaneous laser-assisted machining approaches that rely on continuous laser coupling for localized thermal softening during cutting which requires complex synchronization 49 , the present approach employs laser processing as an independent pre-conditioning stage prior to ultrasonic vibration-assisted micro-milling. This pre-removal reduces the burden of full material engagement along the predefined cutting path, thereby lowering edge loading on the micro-tool and improving engagement stability during subsequent machining.

Taguchi L-16 experimental design is employed to systematically evaluate machining parameters including speed, feed, cutting depth and amplitude. Cutting tools, both coated (TiAlN, TiSiN, nACo) and uncoated, are gauged based on the response variables. An integrated multi-objective optimization framework combining Taguchi Design of Experiments (DOE), Grey Relational Analysis (GRA), and Response Surface Methodology (RSM) is adopted to achieve robust experimental design, simultaneous optimization of multiple machining responses, and predictive modeling of process behavior. Taguchi DOE enables statistically balanced exploration of the machining parameter space with a limited number of experiments, while GRA converts multiple responses into a single Grey Relational Grade (GRG) for unified evaluation. Subsequently, RSM is applied to the computed GRG to establish predictive response models and identify optimum machining conditions within the continuous design space. The combined framework integrates experimental efficiency, multi-response evaluation, and predictive optimization within a unified methodology 50 ,  51 – 52 . ANOVA and regression modeling are used to enumerate the influence of individual factors separately, leading to the determination of the best and worst machining conditions. Finally, validation experiments confirm the optimized settings, ensuring repeatability and reliability of the machining process for high-precision applications.

sections.heading: Selection of material
paragraphs: Unique properties of Inconel 718 have made it the material where conventional materials cannot withstand the rigors of complex, harsh and extreme environments. Seel and aluminum lose their strength in high-temperature and corrosive applications, whereas Inconel 718 keeps its strength over a broad temperature range. Due to its exceptional oxidation resistance and fatigue durability, Inconel 718 operates efficiently at 450–700 °C.

sections.heading: Cutting tool specifications
paragraphs: Selecting appropriate tools for UVAMM of Inconel 718 requires considering material properties, machining conditions, and tool design. Abrasive and heat-resistant nature of Inconel 718 leads to speedy tool wear under intensive forces and temperatures 7 , 55 . Polycrystalline diamond and ceramic coatings for cutting tools have been created exclusively for ultrasonic machining of Inconel 718. Improved tool geometries enhance efficiency by reducing cutting forces and aiding chip evacuation 56 , 57 .

Ultrasonic vibration assisted micro-milling was performed using 500 μm diameter, two-flute tungsten carbide end mills with a helix angle of 30°. All cutting tools employed in this study were supplied by the same manufacturer “Changzhou North Carbide Tool Co., Ltd.” and possessed identical geometrical characteristics to ensure consistent cutting conditions across all experiments. The detailed tool specifications common to all tools, including material, type, overall length, hardness, and helix angle, are summarized in Table  3 .

Table 3 Details and specifications of cutting tool. Specifications Details Material Tungsten carbide Brand name North Carbide Tools Type Square End Carbide Mill Overall length (mm) 50 Rockwell hardness (HRC) 60 Helix angle (°) 30
Fig. 2 Coated and uncoated Tools: (a) Uncoated; (b) TiAlN; (c) TiSiN; (d) nACo.

Tools with three distinct coatings; Titanium Aluminum Nitride (TiAlN), Titanium Silicon Nitride (TiSiN) and AlTiSi-based nanocomposite coating (nACo) were compared to uncoated tools. Figure  2  depicts representative images of the microtools utilized in the experiments, verifying the consistency of tool geometry across all tool conditions. The coating specific properties, such as hardness, thickness, oxidation temperature, and coefficient of friction, are provided in Table  4 . The measured average cutting-edge radii were 2.53 μm for TiAlN coated tools, 2.91 μm for TiSiN coated tools, 2.87 μm for nACo coated tools, and 2.43 μm for uncoated tools. By maintaining identical tool geometry and isolating coating characteristics as the only variable, the experimental design ensures that the observed differences in machining performance can be attributed primarily to coating characteristics rather than geometric variation.

sections.heading: Workpiece preparation
paragraphs: The Inconel 718 workpiece, measuring 10 mm×10 mm×50 mm was clamped in a vice, and its surface was leveled using a 12 mm carbide square end mill. This leveled surface served as the reference for laser-machined pilot slots. After laser machining, the workpiece remained in the same setup and was transferred to the milling center for UVAMM. Tests were performed with a 10 mm cutting length of slot and 3 mm gap between each slot, as illustrated in Fig.  3 .
Fig. 3 Inconel 718 workpiece.

sections.heading: Laser engraving machine
paragraphs: Fiber laser setup Raycus /IPG optional manufactured by Maxphotonics shown in Fig.  4  was used to generate the pilot slots on the leveled workpiece, in the first step. A maximum depth of 0.5 mm can be reached by altering the parameters of the setup like power, frequency and scan speed using Graphical User Interface offered by the Ezcad2 software. The fiber-laser system employed in this study provides independent and flexible control over the principal laser machining parameters, namely laser power, pulse frequency, scanning speed, and loop (pass) count, which are widely recognized as the dominant variables governing laser–matter interaction during slot fabrication. These parameters directly determine the effective energy input per unit length and area, thereby controlling ablation depth, material removal rate, surface morphology, and thermal influence zone during pulsed laser processing of nickel-based superalloys 58 ,  59 ,  60 ,  61 ,  62 – 63 . Descriptions of the laser setup are listed in Table  5 . This parameter-driven control approach aligns with the latest trends in precision laser micromachining of advanced alloys.

Table 5 Details of laser marking machine. Details Specifications Type TS-20 F Power 20 W Laser brand Maxphotonics (Raycus/IPG Optional Marking area 110 mm*100 mm Marking depth (max.) 0.5 mm Marking speed (max.) 7000 mm/s Focus spot diameter < 0.01 mm Output power of laser 10% to 100% (continuously to be adjusted)
Fig. 4 Laser engraving machine.

In laser processing of Inconel 718 and related nickel-based alloys, scanning speed and input laser energy into the workpiece contribute greatly to slot geometry, ablation efficiency and surface quality while pulse frequency dictates the pulse overlap and local heat accumulation with subsequent impact on integrity of materials surface and the formation of recast layer 49 , 64 . In addition, multi-pass (loop-based) laser strategies usually employed for controlled and reproducible slot depth, enabling progressive material removal while reducing excessive recast, debris redeposition and surface instability 65 . Guided by these established principles and supported preliminary trials for stable slot formation, the selected combination of laser parameters guarantees reproducible slot geometry, controlled depth evolution, and sufficient surface conditions for subsequent Ultrasonic Vibration Assisted Micro-Milling (UVAMM).

The laser-generated slots in this study serve as pilot slots in the first phase of a sequential laser hybrid mechanical micro-milling process, while the final slot geometry is produced during the subsequent ultrasonic vibration assisted micro-milling operation. Accordingly, the depth of the laser-machined pilot slots was intentionally maintained approximately 10 μm shallower than the final machined depth. Figure  5  presents representative optical micrographs of laser-generated pilot slots corresponding to different depth levels, together with the laser parameter combinations at which these depths were obtained, as identified through preliminary trials aimed at achieving stable and repeatable pilot slot formation at the targeted depth. The images illustrate the pilot slot geometry and the visible laser-induced thermal influence region adjacent to the slot walls, which is sufficient for evaluating the dimensional constraints of the laser pre-conditioning step within the proposed sequential hybrid machining framework. Detailed microstructural and compositional characterization of the laser-generated slots using SEM and EDS techniques was not undertaken, as the laser-affected material is subsequently removed during the ultrasonic vibration assisted micro-milling stage and does not contribute to the final machined surface condition.
Fig. 5 Laser machined pilot slots for dept: (a) 20 μm; (b) 40 μm; (c) 60 μm; (d) 80 μm with input parameters *(Power (%), Frequency (kHz), Loop Count, Speed (mm/s)).

sections.heading: Milling machine - ultrasonic setup
paragraphs: After engraving pilot slots, work-piece was then machined to the final depth on YDPM Model MV-1060, 3-axis vertical milling center shown in Fig.  6 a. The milling tool was subjected to ultrasonic vibrations using an Acrow Machinery tool holder, operating at 20 kHz with amplitudes between 0 and 10 μm shown in Fig.  6 b. The experimental setup includes an ultrasonic transducer as the primary source of high-frequency vibrations 7 , 66 . High-frequency electrical signals were fed to a transducer that converts this energy into vibrations. These vibrations were subsequently transmitted through an energy-focusing component, such as the horn/tool assembly, inducing high-frequency oscillations along the longitudinal axis. This technique has been employed in numerous works for micro machining of various superalloys including nickel and titanium alloys 67 . Figure  6 c illustrates the use of BMD Messwell 410 V tool pre-setter to achieve precise measurements along the Z axis.
Fig. 6 Experimental setup: (a) machining operation; (b) vertical milling center; (c) tool pre-setter.

sections.heading: Design of experiments
paragraphs: Vibration-assisted machining improves cutting performance, but improper parameter selection can shorten tool life compared to conventional machining. Optimizing milling parameters, including vibration amplitude, frequency and cutting conditions, is essential for achieving stable and predictable machining outcomes 10 . Each process parameter was investigated at four discrete levels, shown in Table  6 , to ensure sufficient coverage of the operating domain and to capture potential nonlinear and transition behaviors characteristic of micro-milling of Inconel 718. The input ranges of the process parameters: spindle speed (6–10.5 m/min), feed per tooth (0.25–1 μm/tooth), and depth of cut (30–90 μm), were selected to span the micro-milling scale where minimum uncut chip thickness, ploughing–shearing transition, tool–workpiece contact mechanics, burr formation sensitivity, and surface integrity evolve significantly. Similar parameter windows have been reported in prior micro-milling studies on Inconel 718 and comparable high-strength alloys with comparable cutting tools and scale. Ultrasonic vibration amplitudes up to 9 μm are consistent with vibration-assisted milling literature, emphasizing improved intermittency and chip breaking. This four-level scheme offers adequate resolution to meaningful identification of trends and robust optimization, while maintaining feasible experimental cost 68 , 69 .

Table 6 Levels of input variables for ultrasonic micro-milling. Process parameters Level 1 Level 2 Level 3 Level 4 Speed ( V c,  m/min) 6 7.5 9 10.5 Feed ( f z , µm/tooth) 0.25 0.5 0.75 1 Depth of Cut ( ap ,  µ m) 30 50 70 90 Tool Coatings Uncoated TiAlN TiSiN nACo Amplitude of vibration ( µ m) 0 3 6 9

Taguchi method uses orthogonal arrays to optimize factor levels, eliminating the need for full factorial experiments while minimizing the number of trials. By focusing on critical experimental runs, it enhances efficiency in analysis and widely applied to optimize machining, minimizes variations and improves process robustness against environmental and component fluctuations 65 . An experimental layout based on Taguchi L16 orthogonal array was developed which analyzes 4 input parameters at 4 levels each, to achieve a practical balance between experimental economy and multi-factor coverage. Full factorial designs (4 5  = 1024 runs) are impractical in hybrid micro-milling due to time and cost constraints, whereas the selected L16 array reduces this requirement to just 16 experiments and allows robust estimation of main effects, which is sufficient for screening and optimization under controlled experimental conditions with confirmation tests to validate the attained results. Although Taguchi L16 orthogonal array is inherently limited in resolving all interaction effects due to aliasing/confounding, this design is well established for screening and optimization in machining research. Therefore, interaction-related interpretations are treated cautiously, and the discussion emphasizes statistically supported main effects validated by confirmation tests, following established practice in machining optimization literature 54 , 70 ,  71 – 72 . Surface roughness, tool wear and burr formation were marked as the response (output) variables. ANOVA was employed to examine the contribution of input parameters to these responses.

sections.heading: Measurement of responses
paragraphs: L-UVAMM, a twostep approach was conducted, and final milled slots were investigated for response variables by using DSX-1000 Olympus Digital Microscope with software version 1.1.5, shown in Fig.  7 a and b, respectively. Measurements of surface roughness, tool wear and burr formation were made and documented for subsequent analysis.
Fig. 7 Measurement setup: (a) digital microscope; (b) representative slot for Surface roughness measurement.

sections.heading: Results and discussions
paragraphs: Each experimental condition was conducted twice under identical conditions using a new tool to eliminate wear effects. Table  7  displays the response values of these experimental runs. Due to the high sensitivity of micromachining, even minor errors and noise significantly impact outcomes. Variations between initial and subsequent runs were attributed to human error, tool quality, and machine noise. Measured data was analyzed using ANOVA and the contribution ratios using a lower-the-better approach were considered to determine parameter significance 73 . Before conducting an analysis of variance (ANOVA), the underlying assumptions of the method were carefully examined, including normality of residuals, homogeneity of variance among factor levels and independence of observations 74 , 75 . Normality was verified through residual distribution analysis and normal probability plot, while variance homogeneity was challenged by the residual-versus-fit plots. The experimental design ensured independence of observations through controlled and randomized experimental trials. The diagnostics confirmed the data suitability for applying ANOVA, thereby ensuring the statistical validity and reliability of the reported F-values, p-values, and contribution ratios. Parameters yielding p-values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant at the 95% confidence level 44 , 76 . ANOVA results for best and worst machining conditions were validated using confirmatory tests. A thorough understanding of material behavior, tool alternatives and process parameters is imperative to optimize the UVAMM of Inconel 718 7 .

The mechanisms governing tool wear and burr formation during laser hybrid ultrasonic micro-milling of Inconel 718 are explained by systematically measured physical responses and validated parametric trends. Tool wear, burr sizes, and surface roughness were measured quantitatively on the machined slots using high resolution digital microscope, while representative micrographs in subsequent sections are provided to describe the measurement approach and typical observed features. The correlations between these physical responses and the governing parameters forms the basis for interpreting the underlying machining behavior. Such an interpretation framework, in which machining behavior is inferred from measured physical responses and their dependence on process parameters, is widely adopted in micro-milling research for nickel-based superalloys, including Inconel 718 77 , 78 .

Compared with conventional micro-milling of Inconel 718, ultrasonic vibration-assisted micro-milling alters the cutting kinematics by superimposing high-frequency oscillations on the tool motion, resulting in intermittent tool–workpiece contact. This intermittent engagement reduces effective contact time and frictional sliding, promotes chip segmentation, and suppresses ploughing-dominated deformation at the micro-scale, leading to improved surface finish and reduced burr formation 19 , 48 . The same mechanism lowers average cutting forces by reducing frictional resistance and effective shear deformation per engagement, which in turn moderates tool wear progression. Thermal behavior is also moderated, as reduced frictional work and periodic tool–work separation decrease heat generation and facilitate improved heat dissipation from the cutting zone 79 ,  80 – 81 .

Within the proposed L-UVAMM framework, the laser-generated pilot slots establish a pre-conditioned engagement path prior to ultrasonic vibration-assisted micro-milling. Consequently, the ultrasonic stage operates under modified engagement conditions rather than directly on untreated bulk material, thereby improving intermittent cutting stability and chip-removal behavior during subsequent machining. The combined interaction between laser pre-conditioning and ultrasonic intermittent cutting therefore establishes a modified hybrid cutting environment fundamentally different from conventional simultaneous laser-assisted machining approaches primarily based on transient thermal softening during cutting. These interaction-driven effects indicate that the proposed L-UVAMM framework influences not only machining performance, but also the underlying chip-formation stability, burr evolution behavior, and tool–workpiece interaction mechanisms governing material removal during micro-milling of Inconel 718.

sections.heading: Surface roughness analysis
paragraphs: Surface roughness is main challenge in micro-milling, affecting the precision and service life of miniaturized components 82 . Conventional machining often struggles to achieve low surface roughness due to interrupted force phenomenon, particularly in aircraft component manufacturing. Roughness is prejudiced by tool geometry, machine accuracy, cooling conditions, undeformed chip thickness and tool wear 83 , 84 . Studies indicate that ultrasonic vibration cutting with coated carbide tools improves surface roughness, extends tool life and reduces wear 85 . Surface roughness was quantified using the areal arithmetic mean height (Sa), which provides a more representative characterization of micro-milled surfaces by capturing height variations across the measured area rather than along a single profile. Areal parameters are particularly suitable under micro-milling conditions where ploughing and shearing mechanisms coexist 86 . Representative areal surface map together with the selected evaluation area used for Sa calculation which corroborates the reported roughness values, are illustrated in Fig.  7 b.

Key process parameters such as cutting speed, feed rate, depth of cut and vibration frequency significantly impact surface finish 7 , 47 . Surface roughness while machining hard materials like Inconel 718, increases with greater feed and depth of cut but decreases at higher speeds 87 , 88 . However, using a lower feed rate with smaller cutting edge radius result reduced residual height of the machined surface 83 . ANOVA results on surface roughness, as presented in Table  8 , identifies cutting speed as the most influential factor, accounting for 26.14% of the overall variability. According to Platt et al. 89 , this impact is primarily due to temperature variations in the cutting zone at higher speeds. Feed rate emerges as the second most significant factor, contributing 20.14% to the variability, closely aligning with the 19.88% impact of tool coatings. In contrast, vibration amplitude and depth of cut exhibit comparatively smaller effects, contributing 12.87% and 12.39%, respectively. As depicted in Fig.  8 , the main effect plots indicate that cutting speed and feed has nonlinear relationship with surface roughness. Initially, surface roughness rises during the transition when speed increases from 6 to 7.5 m/min. However, as speed advances to the higher range of 7.5 to 10.5 m/min, a downward trend emerges, indicating an improvement in surface quality. Lower values of roughness were observed at higher feed rates. Previous studies suggest that the impact of depth of cut on surface roughness remains unpredictable and challenging to assess due to inconsistent findings 90 . Increasing trend in roughness has been observed with more cutting depths. Deeper milling depths induce microcracks due to overheating, further degrading surface quality 46 . Research confirms that increasing vibration amplitude 91  and frequency can enhance surface morphology and reduce roughness as also illustrated in Fig.  8 . Researchers found that reducing tool wear leads to notable improvements in surface quality 92 .
Fig. 8 Surface roughness against machining parameters and tool coatings.

sections.heading: Tool wear analysis
paragraphs: Understanding the tool wear mechanisms is important for optimizing machining performance, tool longevity, part quality and cost efficiency 93 . Flank wear is the most important among different wear types because it leads to cutting edge stability and dimensional accuracy, which are due to mechanical, thermal and chemical stresses 94 . Vibration-assisted machining provides a promising approach to solve this problem by introducing cyclic tool-workpiece separation, improved chip removal and reducing friction and wear 95 . However, control of improper parameters in ultrasonic machining of Inconel 718 increase tool wear 22 , 25 . Studies have demonstrated the advantages of ultrasonic machining over conventional machining as it enhances surface quality and minimizes tool wear 96 , while similar reductions in cutting forces and cutting-zone temperatures have also been reported for titanium alloys 97 . Both vibration frequency and amplitude significantly influence tool-workpiece separation. Increasing vibration amplitude reduces cutting forces even up to 48% and extends tool life 98 , 99 . Comparisons between ultrasonic vibration-assisted and conventional micro-milling further indicate that vibration reduces cutting edge wear and prevents built-up edge formation, thereby enhancing tool longevity and surface quality. Further investigations are essential to fully optimize the advantages of ultrasonic machining in mitigating tool wear 100 .
Fig. 9 Tool wear: (a) uncoated; (b) TiAlN; (c) TiSiN; (d) nACo.

Tool wear was evaluated through analysis of both flank wear and face wear to capture the dominant wear modes occurring during ultrasonic vibration assisted micro-milling. Flank wear is quantified on the clearance face of the cutting tool adjacent to the main cutting edge while face wear is observed and analyzed on the rake face resulting from chip–tool interaction, in accordance with standard wear characterization practice in micro-milling 101 ,  102 – 103 . After each machining trial, worn tools were examined under consistent magnification using a digital microscope. Representative optical micrographs with annotated flank and face wear regions are provided in Fig.  9  to illustrate the wear measurement locations and improve reproducibility of the methodology.

Ultrasonic vibration cutting method demonstrates superior performance in machining tough materials, particularly at low cutting speeds and high tool frequency and amplitude. Increasing cutting speed results in a higher tool workpiece contact ratio, significantly impacting cutting force and tool wear, aligning with theoretical predictions 104 . Table  9  present the ANOVA results, while Fig.  10  illustrates the main effect plots showing tool flank and face wear variations with input parameters. Cutting speed is identified as the most influential factor, contributing 32.22% to tool flank wear, followed by feed (27.75%), amplitude (18.40%) and tool coatings (12.17%). Depth of cuts has the least impact at 8.26%. The minimal error of 1.21% confirms the accuracy of the results 73 . For face wear, cutting speed and tool coating contributed the most by 24.51% and 38.86%, respectively. These findings highlight the dominant contribution of both cutting dynamics and coating materials on tool wear mechanisms in precision micromachining.
Fig. 10 Main effect plot of tool wear: (a) flank wear; (b) face wear.

Figure  11  explains the trends of the responses against each input parameter separately. Both types of wear increased with the rising cutting speed. Excessive heat buildup results in tool material softening which causes adhesion and diffusion 105 . Lower speeds in ultrasonic machining reduces tool wear due to intermittent cutting while at high speeds, the tool stays in more contact with workpiece negating the vibration benefits and increasing tool wear. Efficient ultrasonic-assisted milling of Inconel 718 requires an optimal feed rate, considering its high strength and rigidity of milling setup and cutting tools. Experimental studies have been carried out to determine the ideal feed rate for reduced tool wear and desired surface finish. Research also explores the influence of feed on cutting forces in ultrasonic machining, with the Taguchi method identifying key cutting parameters affecting performance 66 , 85 . Tool wear increases with higher feed due to a rise in undeformed chip thickness and shear plane area, leading to higher material removal rates and greater normal force, a trend observed in multiple studies, including Cui et al. 106 .
Fig. 11 Main effect plots for responses against: (a) cutting speed; (b) feed; (c) depth of cut; (d) tool coatings; (e) amplitude.

The depth of cut plays a critical part in the ultrasonic machining of Inconel 718, directly influencing cutting forces, material removal rate, heat generation and tool wear. A deeper cut increases cutting pressure and tool wear while accelerating material removal, whereas a shallower cut reduces cutting forces and tool wear but slows down machining 20 , 107 . Optimal determination of cutting depth is important for balancing material characteristics, cutting tool capacity and material removal rate to obtain optimal surface quality and tool life 7 , 85 . Prior studies verified that with increasing cutting depth, the tool wear rises because of larger area of shear plane resulting in high material removal rate and temperature in cutting zone, which intensifies resistance to tool. This pattern has been well documented by researchers such as Sui et al. 108 . Figure  11 e illustrates a decline in tool wear as the amplitude increases, with highest wear observed under conventional machining condition at 0 μm amplitude. It displays a 24.74% and 19.46% decrease in flank and face wear, respectively, at an amplitude of 9 μm as compared to conventional machining condition 73 . This reduction is attributed to intermittent tool workpiece interaction in ultrasonic machining, which reduces cutting time, minimizing heat buildup resulting better cooling. Comparable results have been reported by Feng et al. 109  and Liu et al. 110 . Previous research highlights that the ultrasonic vibration cutting method is most effective at low speeds and with high frequency and amplitude 104 . Optimizing these parameters is essential for improved chip breaking, reduced cutting forces and enhanced material removal rates in Inconel 718 machining 111 .

Although coated tools generally exhibit superior wear resistance under conventional machining conditions due to their enhanced hardness and thermal stability, the comparatively lower wear observed for uncoated tools in the present study appears closely associated with the thermo-mechanical interaction conditions established under the proposed L-UVAMM framework. Within the proposed sequential hybrid approach, laser-generated pilot slots reduce severe full-engagement cutting conditions, while ultrasonic vibration-assisted micro-milling introduces repetitive intermittent contact and cyclic thermal interaction during material removal 25 , 98 . Under such conditions, coated tools become increasingly susceptible to localized delamination, edge chipping, micro-fracture, and coating-interface degradation at the micro-scale 55 , 96 . Furthermore, coating deposition modifies the effective cutting-edge geometry, which becomes increasingly significant when coating thickness represents a comparatively larger proportion of the cutting-edge radius 2 , 103 . In contrast, uncoated carbide tools maintain comparatively sharper effective cutting edges and avoid coating-interface failure mechanisms under the proposed hybrid intermittent cutting environment. These observations suggest that the comparatively improved wear performance of uncoated tools is closely associated with the intermittent thermo-mechanical interaction conditions established under the proposed L-UVAMM framework. Tool-wear progression therefore appears strongly influenced by the interaction between intermittent cutting behavior, cyclic thermo-mechanical loading, and coating integrity at the micro-scale.

sections.heading: Burr formation analysis
paragraphs: Inconel 718 tends to form large burrs during micro-milling due to its high plasticity, adhesion and chip-breaking challenges, affecting part accuracy and performance. Burr formation is affected by cutting parameters and tool geometry 69 , 112 . Burrs reduce dimensional precision and require costly post-processing operations, sometimes introducing residual stress especially for micro-components as small size makes them highly susceptible to damage during machining 92 . UVAMM enhances chip breaking, reduces burr formation and improves surface quality while minimizing tool wear, particularly at low speeds, high amplitudes and large feeds 2 , 69 .

Burr formation is more prominent towards the down milling side as compared to the up-milling side, with larger burr width and height. This occurs because the localized cutting-edge velocity on the up-milling side is consistently higher than on the down milling side, leading to increased burr formation in down milling. Previous studies have reported similar findings in micro-milling research 113 . To consider the worst-case scenario, top burrs on the down milling side were analyzed only by measuring the maximum burr width and height identified for each run. The measurement approach for both burr width and burr height is illustrated in Fig.  12 a, where the reference directions and measurement locations are explicitly annotated. Burr width was measured as the horizontal extension of the burr relative to the slot wall,, as shown in Fig.  12 b, whereas burr height was determined as the vertical protrusion of the burr above the surface following established measurement practice 114 .
Fig. 12 Burr measurement: (a) measurement approach; (b) measurement of burr width.

Table  10  displays ANOVA results on burr width and height, along with their contribution ratios. Cutting speed and tool coating are the most significant factors with contribution ratios of 31.35% and 34.40%, respectively. Contribution of the amplitude in both types of burrs is same with a ratio of 23%.

Figure  13  shows main effect plots against each parameter. A larger burr width and height is produced at elevated speeds as a consequence of workpiece deformation because of the higher cutting zone temperatures 89 . Due to nonlinear behavior in burr width, feed contributes the least because its value was higher at first, then dropped and produced high values at higher feed levels while in case of burr height it continuously increased with the feed. This occurs because, at a lower feed, the ploughing effect becomes more prominent, causing the material to undergo plastic deformation and generate larger burrs 115 . A high depth of cut produces less burr than a small depth of cut because burr is type of uncut chips and as the depth of cut increases, the length of chips grows as well, making it easier to chip off from the working piece 78 . Lower values of burr size were seen initially with the rise of amplitude values and at 9 μm, burr width and height were at higher edge, indicating unstable interaction of tool-workpiece due to excessive amplitude. TiAlN and TiSiN coated tools exhibited the best performance for the burrs while uncoated and nACo coated tools showed higher burr values. These burr trends further suggest that the combined interaction between laser pre-conditioning and ultrasonic intermittent cutting promotes more stable chip initiation and separation by reducing severe full-engagement conditions, thereby reducing the tendency for adhesion-dominated side flow and plastic deformation during micro-milling under the proposed L-UVAMM conditions.
Fig. 13 Main effect plots of (a) burr width; (b) burr height.

sections.heading: Optimization of individual process responses
paragraphs: Single-objective optimization targets solely one outcome, often using the ‘smaller is better’ strategy, without addressing potential conflicts with other factors like surface roughness, tool wear, or burr formation. Analysis through main effect plots showed that the best outcomes change with different parameter settings. To authenticate the experimental Taguchi design, confirmatory tests were conducted using the best and worst parameter combinations, with results presented in Table  11 . Optimal combination of input parameters for individual response. These findings are in conformity with anticipated trends from the Taguchi design of experiments and endorsed the experimental technique employed. The analysis also emphasizes that the optimal input levels are distinctive for each response, thus an improvement in one parameter negatively impacts another. This compromise highlights the importance of multi-objective optimization, which reconciles competing targets to provide a comprehensive and effective resolution for practical machining problems 50 , 51 , 116 .

sections.heading: Multi-objective optimization using GRA
paragraphs: Multi-objective optimization (MOO) is vital and widely used decision making technique in situations where multiple conflicting objectives need to be addressed simultaneously, when single-objective optimization methods are inadequate to yield satisfactory solutions. Analysis presented in Table  11  is based on main effect plots shown in Figs.  10  and  13 , reveals that the optimization of any individual output response is dependent on different input parametric conditions. An integrated optimization strategy based on Taguchi Design of Experiments (DOE), Grey Relational Analysis (GRA) and Response Surface Methodology (RSM) was adopted to perform productive multi-response optimization within the laser hybrid ultrasonic micro-milling framework 51 , 52 , 117 . The Taguchi DOE is initially used to systemically organize the experimental configuration and achieve orthogonal coverage of the predetermined multi-factor space so that main effects of each response can be efficiently estimated and evaluated for individual response with minimum number of runs. This criterion balances parametric exploration and statistical reliability for practical experimental constraints. Hence, the Grey Relational Analysis (GRA) is applied to transition multiple individual responses into a single integrated performance metric, namely the Grey Relational Grade (GRG). Taking the use of weight factors into consideration to suitably handle conflicted objectives; GRA, which originates from Grey System Theory, is well established choice for addressing machining optimization, especially when responses have different scales or units as well as their desired trends.

Last, Response Surface Methodology (RSM) is implemented on the computed ‘GRG’ to formulate continuous predictive models over their design space. RSM makes it possible to produce response surfaces, contour plots and regression equations that allow for interpolation, determination of optimum conditions and interpretation of parameter sensitivities. Therefore, the developed integrated Taguchi-GRA-RSM approach complements effective design, multi-response analysis and predictive modeling in a statistically rigorous yet computationally feasible framework for enhancement of performance of hybrid micro-milling processes. Unlike other complex multi-objective optimization techniques, GRA is simple, computationally efficient, and easy to implement. The approach for multi-objective optimization is explained in Fig.  14 . The process of implementing GRA in multi objective optimization follows a systematic approach that includes preprocessing and normalization of data, computation of Grey Relational Coefficients (GRCs) and Grey Relational Grades (GRGs). GRA, based on the Taguchi method, reduces a multi-response problem to a single unique function 118 , 119 .
Fig. 14 Scheme for multi objective optimization.

GRA-based optimum represents the best observed experimental condition, whereas the RSM-based optimum represents the model-predicted optimum in the continuous design space. Minor discrepancies between these two solutions are expected and reflect the complementary nature of the two optimization approaches rather than methodological conflict. For practical application, the GRA solution provides a reliable experimentally validated parameter set, while the RSM solution serves as a refined optimization guide for further process improvement.

Meta-heuristic optimization techniques such as Genetic Algorithms, Particle Swarm Optimization, Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II, and Grey Wolf Optimizer are also widely applied for solving complex, nonlinear, and multi-objective optimization problems in machining and manufacturing 120 ,  121 – 122 , and have been shown to effectively explore global optima in large search spaces. However, these approaches typically require a large number of function evaluations or iterations to converge and extensive computational or surrogate modeling, which are particularly effective in simulation-based studies but impose substantial experimental burden associated with physical machining trials and cost constraints when applied on high-cost alloys such as Inconel 718 123 , 124 .

paragraphs: The alternatives are ranked based on their GRG values. The alternative with higher GRG indicates a better alternative while lower GRG have weaker relational closeness to the ideal solution. The best-ranked alternative is considered the most optimal choice in the decision-making process. Experimental runs along with their GRG values are displayed in Table  12 . Highest GRG value was realized for Test No. 02 with TiAlN coated tool having cutting speed at 6 m/min, feed at 0.5 μm/tooth, depth of cut at 50 μm and amplitude at 3 μm.

sections.heading: Response surface methodology (RSM)
paragraphs: RSM is a powerful analytical approach for optimizing processes influenced by multiple variables and their interactions. This methodology enables continuous refinement and enhancement of experimental processes by leveraging statistical and mathematical modeling 125 . Unlike the Taguchi Method, RSM integrates experimental design, statistical analysis, and data-fitting techniques to achieve more precise and effective process optimization.

sections.heading: Regression analysis
paragraphs: Regression analysis is a statistical technique used to establish the relationship between multiple dependent and independent factors simultaneously. It is particularly useful in multi-objective optimization, where multiple conflicting objectives must be balanced to achieve the best possible solution. The regression-based optimization involved regression modeling of multi-objective function, ANOVA for model validation and Optimization using RSM.

sections.heading: Regression modeling of multi-objective function
paragraphs: Contour plots assess the relationship between two independent variables and their influence on the predicted response. Figure  15  show contour plots for all four tools that demonstrate the dependence of the GRG on input parameters. These graphical representations illustrate the synergistic effect of process parameters on GRG. It is observed that the maximum GRG values are obtained with low cutting speed and feed rates.
Fig. 15 Contour plots of GRG vs. machining conditions for tools: (a) uncoated; (b) TiAlN; (c) TiSiN; (d) nACo.

sections.heading: ANOVA for model validation
paragraphs: The performance improvement and statistical adequacy of the developed Grey Relational Grade (GRG) regression models was rigorously evaluated using established goodness-of-fit metrics, comprehensive diagnostic analysis, and experimental reliability. The model performance indicators, including R² (96.90%), adjusted R 2  (94.94%), predicted R 2  (91.08%), statistical significance and contribution of each factor, are summarized in Table  13 , demonstrating good model adequacy, predictive capability, and statistical reliability of the developed GRG regression model 126 . It provides an overview of the ANOVA results for the response variables, highlighting that tool coating is the most significant factor affecting the GRG, with a contribution of 46.92%. Cutting speed follows with a 29.97% contribution, while depth of cut and amplitude had minimal individual impact.

Further validation was conducted through detailed residual diagnostics, as illustrated in Fig.  16 . The normal probability plot and histogram indicate that the residuals follow an approximately normal distribution, the residuals versus fitted value plot confirms variance homogeneity with no systematic patterns, and the residuals versus observation order plot demonstrates the independence of errors 127 . In addition, validation experiments at the RSM-predicted optimal parameters demonstrated clear performance improvements. Collectively, these statistical and graphical assessments thereby strengthen the reliability, and statistical authenticity of the developed GRG regression models and the associated optimization conclusions.
Fig. 16 Residual diagnostics of the GRG regression model: (a) Normal probability plot; (b) Residuals versus fits; (c) Histogram of residuals; (d) Residuals versus observation order.

sections.heading: Regression model optimization
paragraphs: After validation of regression model developed in Eq. ( 5 ) through ( 8 ), it was optimized through RSM to get optimal machining conditions. RSM is a mathematical and statistical technique that models and optimizes processes where multiple input variables influence an output response. With a 95% confidence level, the response surface optimizer projected the optimal parameter combination for maximized GRG, which yielded the lowest value of surface roughness, tool wear, and burr formation. Figure  17  displays the input parameter settings ( Vc = 6 m/min ,  fz = 0.6 μm/tooth ,  ap = 60 μm ,  TiAlN coated tool ,  A = 8 μm ) for the optimized output. Additional experimentation was conducted to validate the results.
Fig. 17 Response Surface Optimization against GRG for input conditions. * 2 = TiAlN Coated.

sections.heading: Validation experiments
paragraphs: The effectiveness of the optimized machining conditions was evaluated by comparing with the best experimental run Test No. 02, as detailed in Table  14 . Notable improvements across all responses are observed with the optimized parameters. Surface roughness exhibited the most significant reduction of 43.96%, followed by 34.31% and 20.05% decrease in flank and face wear, respectively. Additionally, burr width and height were lowered by 13.56% and 25.74%, highlighting the enhanced machining performance.

Experimental variability is unavoidable in micro-milling because of tool wear evolution, material inconsistency, and measurement uncertainty. The validity and robustness of the obtained optimization results were therefore scrutinized with several statistical criteria including ANOVA, residuals analysis, coefficient of determination (R 2 ) and 95% confidence intervals for predicted response. Validation trials performed at optimal parameter settings additionally support the consistency in improved trends, dictating that the optimized solution is robust against inherent experimental variability.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Successful experimental investigation has been conducted herein to bridge the identified gap by scrutinizing a set of combination levels of machining parameters in conjunction with various tool coatings for laser hybrid ultrasonic vibration assisted mechanical micro-milling of super alloy Inconel 718. ANOVA and GRA were adopted to analyze the measured outcomes to pattern the impact of each input parameter on surface roughness, tool wear, and burr formation. The findings of this study as summarized below offer a substantial contribution by elucidating the intricate interdependencies among machining parameters, tool coatings and their profound influence on surface integrity, tool degradation, and burr control. These insights emphasize the need for judicious tool coating selection and meticulous parametric optimization to augment surface finish, enhance tool efficiency, and promote operational sustainability.

Target depths of laser-generated pilot slots were achieved by controlling power, scan speed, loop count, and frequency. Higher frequency and power ensured consistent slot formation by reducing recast layers and debris. Cutting speed, feed/tooth, depth of cut, tool coatings, and amplitude contributed 26.14%, 20.14%, 12.39%, 19.88%, and 12.87% respectively to surface roughness. TiAlN coatings produced the lowest roughness while nACo yielded the highest. Roughness decreased with higher cutting speed and amplitude, increased with depth of cut and varied nonlinearly with feed due to thermal softening. Flank wear was affected by cutting speed (32.22%) and feed (27.75%), whereas face wear was governed by tool coatings (38.86%). Flank wear increased with all factors except amplitude due to intermittent cutting phenomena. Face wear declined initially then raised with feed and depth, decreased with amplitude and increased with speed due to cutting zone temperatures. Uncoated tools outperformed the coated ones, with nACo tools exhibiting the highest wear. Cutting speed (31.35%) and amplitude (23.63%) were dominant for burr width while burr height was influenced by speed (25.73%) and amplitude (23.47%). Burr width increased with speed and feed but decreased with depth; amplitude first reduced then increased it due to incomplete chip separation and tool instability. Burr height followed similar pattern for amplitude, decreasing with feed and depth but rising with speed. TiSiN minimized burr height, TiAlN minimized burr width whereas nACo performed worst in both. GRA identified the optimal conditions as 6 m/min speed, 0.5 μm feed/tooth, 50 μm depth and 3 μm amplitude with TiAlN tools while the worst performance occurred with nACo at 10.5 m/min, 0.75 μm feed, 50 μm depth and 0 μm amplitude. ANOVA of Regression model against GRG identified tool type as the most influential factor (45.76%) followed by speed (28.69%). RSM identified optimal parameters as 6 m/min cutting speed, 0.6 μm/tooth feed, 60 μm depth, and 8 μm amplitude with TiAlN tools. Under these optimized machining conditions, validation experiments confirmed 43.95%, 34.31%, 20.05%, 13.56%, and 25.74% reduction in surface roughness, flank wear, face wear, burr width, and burr height, respectively, thereby verifying the effectiveness of the proposed optimization strategy across all targeted performance objectives.

sections.heading: Future work
paragraphs: Based on this experimental research work, the following future research directions are anticipated to further enhance understanding and development in the field of hybrid micromachining.

Expansion of the current work by incorporating microstructural and compositional characterization techniques including Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy, to analyze the laser-induced alterations in more detail. Such an analysis would be especially beneficial for stand-alone laser machining or alternate hybrid process configurations, where laser-affected material contributes directly to the final surface condition. Direct experimental comparison of the proposed sequential laser hybrid ultrasonic vibration assisted micro-milling framework with conventional and single-assistance machining approaches under identical machining conditions could be conducted in future for more rigorous evaluation of machining efficiency in tool wear, and surface quality. Such comparative studies will further clarify the relative advantages and application potential of the proposed hybrid machining strategy. Integration of meta-heuristic optimization techniques, such as Genetic Algorithms and NSGA-II, with hybrid modeling frameworks to enable global multi-objective optimization of micro-milling processes. Such approaches would facilitate efficient exploration of complex and highly nonlinear design spaces, complement the present statistical framework, and further enhance optimization robustness. This direction is expected to broaden the applicability and optimization capability of machining strategies for difficult-to-machine materials.
